The Purple-backed thornbill (Ramphomicron microrhynchum) is a diminutive Andean hummingbird whose life history presents striking energetic optimizations. At a typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the species exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 14.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 14.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the extreme metabolic demands of hovering flight at high altitudes. Field records indicate that neonatal chicks emerge from their incubated eggs at a remarkably low mass of only 0.66 grams [Wwb = 0.66 grams], a trait that aligns with the altricial developmental mode common among trochilids. This initial body mass stands in stark contrast to the ultimate adult dimensions, as sexually mature females attain an ultimate wet weight of 9.8 grams [Wwi = 9.8 grams] while males, exhibiting a slight dimorphism, reach a larger ultimate wet weight of 10.1 grams [Wwi = 10.1 grams]. Such size differences are modest but consistent with the species’ monogamous breeding system and the intense aerodynamic constraints of its high-elevation habitat.

Developmental timing in this species is tightly coupled to thermal conditions experienced during incubation. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] yield an incubation period of 16 days [ab = 16 days], a duration that is comparatively short for a hummingbird of this body size and likely reflects the energetic imperative to minimize exposure to predators in open paramo nests. Once hatched, the altricial nestling follows a rapid developmental trajectory governed by the species’ elevated metabolic regime. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of active metabolic periods at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], fledging occurs at 20 days since birth [tx = 20 days since birth], marking the achievement of flight feather maturation and the capacity for sustained aerial locomotion. This relatively brief nestling phase is characteristic of small-bodied high-altitude trochilids, where early fledging reduces the cumulative predation risk during the vulnerable brooding period.

The onset of reproductive maturity follows a distinctly protracted schedule relative to the rapid early development observed in this species. Puberty, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis and gonadal activation, is attained at 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay in sexual maturation is an adaptive response to the resource-poor environments of the northern Andes, where young birds require a prolonged period of somatic growth and foraging skill acquisition before they can sustain the energetic costs of reproduction. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this age at puberty is near the median for hummingbirds of equivalent body mass, with the temporal lag likely reflecting the need to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to support both the daily resting energetic costs and the substantial energetic investment of the first breeding attempt.

First reproduction, however, occurs considerably later than the attainment of sexual maturity alone would suggest, a pattern that underscores the complex ecological constraints operating on this species. The time since birth at first brood is estimated at approximately 329 days [tR = approximately 329 days] under a stable thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], indicating that individuals defer their initial breeding effort for nearly a full year after reaching puberty. This pronounced lag between gonadal readiness and actual reproductive activity is consistent with observations in other high-elevation Andean birds, where the brief and unpredictable breeding windows impose strong selective pressure for optimal body condition and territory ownership at the time of first nesting. The species’ annual reproductive output is further constrained by its modest clutch size.

Females typically deposit two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate that is low even by hummingbird standards. This conservative strategy is likely a direct consequence of the extreme metabolic costs associated with incubation and chick provisioning at high elevations, where nightly torpor is frequently employed by brooding females to conserve energy. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, measured at 6.8 years [am = 6.8 years] under the thermoneutral conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], is relatively long for a bird of its diminutive size, reflecting the slow pace of life that characterizes many high-altitude tropical organisms. This extended longevity, combined with the deferred onset of reproduction and the minimal annual fecundity, situates Ramphomicron microrhynchum firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among trochilids. Such a suite of demographic traits appears to be an evolutionary response to the chronically low resource availability and high adult survival probabilities that prevail in its paramo and elfin forest habitats.
